summary: The speaker, co-founder and CTO at Orb (a usage-based billing infrastructure company), presents a framework for pricing AI agents, drawing on numerous real-world examples. The talk surveys pricing models across the AI agent landscape: Intercom's Finn uses outcome-based pricing at $0.99 per resolution; Unify employs credits, a pricing calculator, and multiple pricing axes; Cursor appears simple at $20/$40 per month but hides complexity around completions, requests, model tiers, and usage caps; ChargeFlow charges a percentage per recovered chargeback as an ROI guarantee. Key principles include considering the target audience and their buying process, maintaining simplicity and predictability, planning for usage expansion over time, and understanding cost and margin structures. Additional examples illustrate audience considerations: Clay highlights Explorer and Pro tiers with logo gardens; Replit offers a technical, granular pricing page; Heia and ServiceNow use 'book a demo' pages for enterprise sales; AI SDRs use flat monthly rates benchmarkable against human SDR productivity; Devon charges per month plus ACUs. The talk addresses cost and margin structure, citing Jeff Bezos's observation that 'your margin is my opportunity.' Companies should understand cost axes—especially inference—and pass R&D innovation into cost structure. Character AI invested early in inference optimization, sustaining 100 million daily active users. Jasper moved to unlimited credits on paid tiers, enabled by a model decision-making engine selecting among multiple LLM providers. The final principle is pricing flexibility: pricing must be a continuous evolution, not a set-it-and-forget-it exercise. As OpenAI's cost per token decreased drastically, input costs shift and new use cases like healthcare and legal AI become viable. Luma Labs illustrates multiple pricing levers including platform, modes, credits, and rate limits. Prepaid credits offer benefits including immediate cash flow, fraud mitigation, easy discounting via conversion rates, seasonal demand handling, and generalizability from trials to enterprise commitments. For 2025, the speaker predicts continued price wars and a race to the bottom in some verticals, more unlimited plans driven by commoditized inputs, maturation of outcome-based pricing with clearer SLAs, and increased R&D investment in monetization infrastructure including spend controls, usage auditing, and billing systems with versioning and migrations as first-class features.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Speaker introduces themselves as co-founder and CTO at Orb, a usage-based billing infrastructure company, and outlines the talk's focus on pricing AI agents across diverse market segments.

sections.title: Pricing Model Examples Survey
sections.summary: Reviews pricing pages from Intercom/Finn (outcome-based $0.99/resolution), Unify (credits, calculator, hybrid), Cursor (simple surface, complex underneath), and ChargeFlow (outcome-based chargeback recovery percentage).

sections.title: Key Pricing Principles
sections.summary: Introduces core principles: consider target audience and buying process, never compromise simplicity and predictability, and plan for usage expansion over time by encouraging or discouraging specific workloads.

sections.title: Audience-Targeted Pricing Examples
sections.summary: Examines Clay (go-to-market, Explorer/Pro tiers, logo gardens), Replit (developer-focused, technical pricing), Heia and ServiceNow (enterprise 'book a demo'), AI SDRs (flat rate, benchmarkable), and Devon (monthly cost plus ACUs, introducing new buyer paradigm).

sections.title: Cost and Margin Structure
sections.summary: Discusses Jeff Bezos's margin quote, advises against over-indexing on cost, emphasizes understanding cost axes (especially inference), and presents Character AI as an example of early inference investment enabling massive scale.

sections.title: Jasper and Pricing Flexibility
sections.summary: Presents Jasper's move to unlimited credits on paid tiers, enabled by a model decision-making engine selecting among OpenAI, Anthropic, and Cohere to reduce costs. Introduces pricing flexibility as the final and most important principle: pricing cannot be set-it-and-forget-it. Companies should measure willingness to pay continuously as industries mature, inputs change, and product value increases. Contrasts sudden once/twice-yearly pricing changes with continuous pricing evolution that captures increasing product value and brings customers along.

sections.title: Input Cost Evolution and New Use Cases
sections.summary: Shows OpenAI's cost per token decreasing drastically over ~1.5 years, emphasizing that input costs for AI agents shift continuously. Notes that use cases seeming out of reach today (healthcare AI, legal AI with heavy data digestion) may become viable in 1-2 years as token costs decline, affecting both pricing and the product landscape.

sections.title: Luma Labs and Pricing Levers
sections.summary: Uses Luma Labs to illustrate that pricing flexibility extends beyond shifting a dollar price point. Multiple levers exist: platform (web/iOS), mode (relax mode), credit system, and rate limits. Companies should maximize the number of adjustable levers within the bounds of simplicity for their audience.

sections.title: Prepaid Credits Model
sections.summary: Details benefits of prepaid credits: immediate cash flows for COGS-heavy businesses, fraud counteraction through upfront payment, easy discounting via a single credit-to-dollar conversion rate, handling of seasonal demand fluctuations, and generalizability from small-company trials to multi-million-dollar enterprise commitments.

sections.title: 2025 Predictions and Technical Challenges
sections.summary: Predicts continued price wars and a race to the bottom in some verticals, more unlimited plans driven by commoditized inputs and competition, maturation of outcome-based pricing with clearer SLAs and success definitions, and increased R&D investment in monetization infrastructure for usage control, spend caps, and auditing. Notes technical challenges in billing including complex business logic, enterprise agreements, legacy price points, and the need for versioning and migrations as first-class features. Concludes by introducing Orb as a specialized billing engine addressing these challenges.
